BN《Smoke³∙Moon²⁰∙SigS¹⁴∙Niko⁸》-4 has pinned a message to this channel
DM [BN] APP 02-09-2025 04:13 PM
An exquisitely penned invitation arrives at your doorstep, sealed with the crimson mark of Castle Ravenloft. You are cordially invited to the Moonlight Masquerade, hosted by His Most Esteemed Lord, Count Strahd von Zarovich. Join us for an evening where secrets are currency and masks reveal as much as they hide. Pruna's invitation has an additional note written in another hand: I have been watching your every move with keen interest. Your masked presence would be... enlightening, for us both. -S Belvedere's invitation has a postscript that reads: I have seen you walk among the veiled and the garish alike. Tell me, which face is truly yours? Come, we'll have a game of discerning whether the mask you bring is the truth or a lie! -S Rux' invitation has a postscript that reads: I see the silver glow of the moon's favor in your eyes, an uncommon light in these lands. Your attendance is expected. -S MacOonnie's invitation has a postscript that reads: Whispers say you harbor daylight’s touch in a body sworn to night. Present yourself, and we shall learn whether that radiance is discipline, or defiance. -S Seal Credit: https://www.etsy.com/au/listing/709496603/strahd-zadrovich-family-crest-wax-seal (edited)

Belvedere, after reading the invitation, groans. "Why does the Count keep bothering me?" He pinches the bridge of his nose to calm himself down. "A party?! A masquerade of all things? However, if Strahd is going to tease him with vague assertions about challenging truth and lies, there's no way he can refuse to attend. With a sigh, the faithful of Lathander pulls a cloak over his shoulder and heads to the market square in Vallaki -- one of the few places in the valley where he might find something as frivolous as a mask for the masquerade...

Rux Mooneye APP 03-09-2025 04:53 AM
It is early in the morning as Rux receives his invitation. As he rises from the previous night’s slumber terrified whispers flit about, muted by the waterfall running through the cave that he and his pack call their den. The envelope bearing the seal of Barovia’s vampire lord still lay at the entrance, undisturbed by any other werewolves as the sun’s pale light illuminates it, shining as if it were a beacon reaching for the heavens. Feigning as if he had a choice, his decision is quickly made with promises to return. Some time later he finds himself atop Ulua, his lupine steed, dread looming overhead as they enter Vallaki. Flashing smiles to peasants that may be unwary of the presence of a goblin riding a wolf he finds himself entering the market. Never has he been invited to a castle, let alone a party within one. With desperation he hopes he finds a familiar face, one that can help him prepare for this fateful evening.

*Meanwhile, as old friends reconnect, the he Vallaki market is alive with noise and motion. Stalls crowd the square, awnings flapping in the morning breeze. Merchants call out prices on onions, rye bread, and smoked fish. Children dart between tables chasing each other. A fiddler scrapes a tune near the fountain, and for once, the crowd doesn't seem afraid to stop and listen, not like in past years under the Baron. But beneath the bustle, there's an undercurrent of unease. The Wachter banners, red stitched with golden lions, hang over the square, reminders of who truly holds power now. A few people in plain cloaks linger at corners, watching too intently to be simple shoppers. When their eyes sweep the crowd, conversations dip quieter until they pass. Still, the people play along. The illusion of freedom is better than none, it seems.At least people aren't being dragged away for "reformation", right? For now, the market hums with almost normalcy of people going on with their lives.*

A pre-masquerade montage...
DM [BN] APP 12-09-2025 12:18 PM
The manor fills with the bustle of preparation. Doors open and close, boots and shoes scuff against old floorboards, and low murmur of voices rises and falls. Some take time at a cracked mirror, asking others "What do you think of this?" or "is that too much?" Others pull on cloaks and try on masks in quiet corners, keeping their choices hidden until the last moment. A few laughs break the tension, a toast is made, a bottle of Champagne du le Stomp is opened, but nerves are still taut beneath the surface. Day turns to dusk. The sound shifts. A creak outside, heavy. A cold draft slips through the seams of the old walls, carrying the chill of evening. Through the windows, just beyond the gates, a black carriage waits on the road. Two large black horses stomp their feet. The horses snort puffs of steamy breath into the chill mountain air. The side door of the carriage swings open silently.

At the mention of Jander, something subtle changes. The shift is not dramatic -- no flare of temper, no visible crack in composure -- but the warmth in Strahd's eyes cools by a noticeable degree. "It has been some time since I have heard that name spoken without trembling." His gaze sharpens as he studies Mac anew, no longer as a curiosity but as a variable to be conisidered. "You speak of him as though you understood him. Few did." A faint, thinner smile touches his lips. “He was luminous. He mistook that for righteousness. He believed suffering ennobled him, that refusal elevated him, that one might exist as a vampire and remain... uncorrupted.” “He was wrong.” There is no heat, no sharpness to the statement. Only certainty. "He imagined himself untethered," Strahd continues. "As all who tire of gravity eventually do. And he left." The final word is delivered without flourish, but it lands heavily. "You released a shadow of him," Strahd goes on, voice smooth again, almost conversational. "How compassionate. How intersting." The music swells and laughter carries across the hall, masking the shift in tone to outsiders. "Tell me," Strahd says, eyes on Mac's, "when that shadow spoke, did it speak of freedom? Or of regret?" The question hangs between them, polite on its surface and edged beneath. This is no longer about blood or culture. It is about philosophy. How Mac sees Jander will be revealing. Strahd has been close to one idealist before.

And so, the game is afoot! The side door opens with a soft scrape. The air inside the chamber is stale, thick with dust and parchment. Shelves sag under the weight of scroll tubes and brittle tomes. Knee-high piles of papers scatter the floor, leaving narrow paths between several heavy iron-bound chests. The only clear space is the doorway you've entered, a narrow path to the middle of the room, and another narrow path to another door at the end of the room, set into a convex curved wall. At the center of the room, where the two paths from the two doors join, sits a massive black desk buried under ledgers. Perched on a tall stool behind it is a thin, stooped man with pale skin and stringy grey hair. His clothes were once fine, but have long since become worn, threadbare, stained with ink and dulled with parchment dust. A chain runs from a cuff at his ankle to a heavy ring fixed to the desk. He scratches endlessly across a scroll that spills off the desk and runs across the floor. The quill as he writes makes a dry rasping sound. Nearby, a tasseled rope hangs from a small hole in the ceiling. The scratching stops. Slowly, the man lifts his head. His eyes flick from Belvedere, to Pruna, to the door behind them. His gaze lingers on their hands, then their masks, as if cataloguing entries in a ledger. He does not stand. He does not look surprised. Only mildly inconvenienced. ----- Pruna's newly blessed sight sharpens the world instantly. Colors deepen. Edges glow faintly. Even her own hands look... different. He carries the pot with Rux's help through the courtyard, past the impossible sunflowers, and something in his face works quietly the whole way -- the look of a man turning over a thing he has not let himself want in a long time. "Dogs." The larger head says it low, almost to itself. "Had one. Before here. Slept against my back in winter." He stops at the east wing door, keys in his claw, and pauses before inserting the key into the lock. "They'd bark at what they smell. Things here smell wrong. Wouldn't be fair to them, penned up with this." He glances at Rux, and there is something unguarded in it, very briefly. "But you're kind to offer. Ask again when the Abbot's decided about your flowers." He inserts the key into the lock and turns it.

TW: madness ||The sound reaches you as the door opens even just a crack. Howling, but not wolf-howling, and not one but but dozens, layered. Human voices bent unnaturally, cackling that breaks into weeping and back again, a rhythmic thudding of something against a wall, and beneath it all a low constant murmur, like the abbots congregation is "praying," but the words are unintelligible. Inside, the madhouse is worse than the Abbot's gentle framing suggested. Sixty people, maybe more, packed into rooms that were bedchambers once. The feeding goes door by door. Some rooms hold quiet ones who take their bowls with trembling care. Many are not quiet. A few reach through the gaps as the pot passes, not grasping hold, just reaching. One room near the east door holds nine who stare in perfect silence and do not touch their bowls until Clovin has moved on. Pruna's chatter does something Clovin's presence alone does not. Not everywhere -- some rooms wail on regardless -- but here and there, after the initial shrieking at the sight of her, the noise gutters down to listening. A room of brawlers stops mid-scuffle. A woman with a cluster of red spider's eyes across half her face presses close to her door gap and goes still, tracking Pruna's voice. Someone kind, and who pays them attention for who they are. Rux's flavored stew is met with weeping gratitude in some rooms and deep suspicion in others. One man receives his bowl, picks out every piece of turnip, and lays them in a precise, careful row on the floor, each one placed with the attention of a craftsman, before he begins to eat.|| Clovin locks each door behind him without cruelty and without apology, just completing a chore he's done a thousand times. As he closes the and locks the main door to the courtyard, he says to no one in particular. At the last one he stands a moment, keys in his claw, and says, mostly to the pot: "He means well. That's the thing people don't understand about this place." (edited)

Then he shuffles back toward the main hall, and the abbey settles into its version of quiet -- the wind, the creak of the scarecrows on the wall, sixty-odd sleepers behind locked doors, and a ring of sunflowers blazing gold against the dark, waiting for morning and whatever attention it brings. As you walk back through the courtyard, the Abbot's voice reaches you from the main hall -- low, resonant, unhurried. The words are Celestial, timeless, each phrase ringing in the air a half-second longer than it should. It does not pause, and it will not pause for hours, or perhaps even days. Whatever the you might wish for the people behind those locked doors, tonight is not the night. But perhaps there will come a time when the abbot is away, and the moon is dark, do do things without as many watchful eyes.
